# Whatever Comes to Me

I'm sitting at my desk on a Tuesday afternoon, and the light through the window is doing that thing where it makes the dust particles visible. You ever notice how dust only becomes real when the sun hits it just right? It's like those particles were always there, but they needed permission from the light to exist in our awareness. That feels like a metaphor for something important, but I'm not sure what.

There's a coffee cup next to me with cold coffee in it. I think it's from this morning, or maybe yesterday morning. Time has become a little fuzzy lately. Not in a bad way, just in a way where days blend together like watercolors if you add too much water. You're supposed to know the difference between the days, but sometimes I think that's just a convention we agreed to so we wouldn't all lose our minds.

I wonder if other people feel like this, or if I'm alone in finding comfort in the formlessness of time. Probably I'm not alone. That's what the internet has taught me—whatever weird thing you're experiencing, thousands of other people are experiencing it too, and they've probably already written a Reddit post about it.

My neighbor is mowing his lawn for what must be the tenth time this month. I don't know why he mows so much. The grass hasn't changed since the last time. Maybe he's not actually trying to change the grass. Maybe the mowing is the point. Maybe I should be more like him—finding purpose in repetition, finding meaning in the doing rather than the result. Or maybe he just really likes the sound of the mower. I would understand that.

I've been thinking about my childhood lately, which is funny because I haven't thought about it much in years. But something small will happen—I'll find a penny, or I'll see a kid eating a Popsicle, or I'll hear a song that was popular when I was eight—and suddenly I'm back there. And it's strange because I can't remember what I actually thought or felt as that person, even though I was that person. It's like looking at a picture of yourself and not quite recognizing the face, even though you know logically that it's you.

I think about all the versions of myself that have existed. The one at age seven who believed dinosaurs might still exist somewhere. The one at sixteen who was convinced I had it all figured out. The one at twenty-three who thought sadness was actually depth. And now this one, the current one, who isn't sure what he thinks about anything, but that's okay.

Someone once told me that the cells in your body replace themselves every seven years, so technically you're a completely different person every seven years. That means I've been at least five completely different people, with no overlap at all. Except I remember being the others. I have their memories, their feelings, their terrible decisions. So what does that make me? A ghost haunted by my own past?

This is the kind of thought that can spiral, so I'm going to stop it here.

Instead, I'm going to think about something practical. I need to do laundry. I've needed to do laundry for three days now. The clothes are piling up in the corner of my bedroom like a textile stalagmite, growing slowly but inexorably toward the ceiling. Tomorrow I'll do it. Or the day after. Eventually, all my clothes will be dirty, and then I'll have no choice. There's something almost freeing about that inevitability.

I wonder if other people think about laundry as much as I do. I think laundry is actually profound if you think about it in the right way. It's this cycle of cleanliness and dirtiness, with water and heat as the agents of transformation. You put something in broken and dirty, and you take something out restored. It's like baptism or therapy or sleeping. It's a reset button, but for cloth.

I'm being ridiculous now. I know I'm being ridiculous. But there's a pleasure in that too, in letting your mind wander into ridiculous places. It's like giving your thoughts permission to play instead of work.

The sun is moving. I can see it in how the dust particles have shifted, making new geometric patterns in the air. Soon it'll be evening, and then night, and then morning again, and the cycle will continue. The mower will probably come out again next week. The coffee cup will remain on my desk until I remember it exists. My laundry will wait, patient and growing.

And I'll still be here, or a new version of me will be here, thinking thoughts that probably won't matter in a week, or a month, or a year. But they matter now, in this moment, in this specific Tuesday afternoon when the light is doing that thing.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's all we ever have—these small moments of noticing, of being present to the dust and the coffee and the mower outside and the feeling of your own thoughts happening inside your head. Maybe that's the whole point, and we've all been looking for something much more complicated.

Or maybe not. Maybe I'm just someone who hasn't done their laundry and is overthinking things on a Tuesday afternoon.

Either way, it's been nice to sit here and write whatever came to me. Words are strange—they're like fishing, throwing your line out into the void and seeing what you catch. Sometimes it's something beautiful and surprising. Sometimes it's just an old boot. But the act of casting the line—that's always worth something.

The afternoon is getting late now. Soon I should do something productive. Or not. Maybe I'll just sit here a little longer and let the dust be real in the sunlight.
